sections.h2: Where is the Hamilton County Recorder's Office, and when can I file a deed?
sections.html:
The Hamilton County Recorder's Office sits at 138 East Court Street, Room 205, in downtown Cincinnati. Public hours run Monday to Friday, 7:30 AM to 4:00 PM, and the recording desk takes new filings from 7:30 AM to 3:30 PM.

The same address handles mail. Anything sent in for return needs a self-addressed, stamped envelope, and the office says turnaround is typically two to three business days. Blank forms are not sold at the counter, so a deed has to come from your attorney, your title company or your own preparation.

The Recorder's site also says staff cannot run searches for customers. If you need a title search, hire a title examiner or a title company. Staff will show you how to use the online index, which is free to browse along with document images.

sections.h2: What kind of county is Hamilton County, Ohio, for a property owner?
sections.html:
Hamilton County is Ohio's southwestern corner, with Cincinnati as the seat and largest city, and it is the third most populous county in the state. It covers 413 square miles, including about 406 of land, along the Ohio River valley with the Great Miami River, Little Miami River and Mill Creek feeding its hills and valleys.

The county was organized in 1790 as the second county of the Northwest Territory, which is why the Recorder's website can offer scanned deed books reaching back to 1794. Few Ohio offices hold land records that old.

  • Population: 838,418 in the Census Bureau's July 1, 2025 estimate, up from 830,639 at the 2020 census.
  • Housing: 383,689 housing units, with 59.3% of occupied homes owner-occupied (2020 to 2024).
  • Median value of an owner-occupied home: $241,900 for 2020 to 2024.
  • Median gross rent: $1,075, and 1,162 building permits were issued in 2025.

Source: Census Bureau QuickFacts for Hamilton County and the county's Wikipedia entry for geography and history.

sections.h2: In what order does a Hamilton County deed move through the county offices?
sections.html:
A conveyance goes to the County Auditor first, then to the Recorder. The Recorder's FAQ states that mailed conveyances are accepted only when the Engineer's and Auditor's stamps are already on the document, and the office will not carry a deed through those two offices for you.

  1. Prepare the deed, signed and acknowledged under Ohio law.
  2. Complete the Auditor's conveyance form (DTE Form 100 for a taxable transfer, DTE Form 100 EX for an exempt one).
  3. Deliver the deed, forms and fee to the Auditor's Transfer Desk, 138 East Court Street, Room 304.
  4. Collect the stamped deed and file it with the Recorder, along with a stamped return envelope if the Recorder is to mail it back.

The Auditor's Transfer Desk is open 7:30 AM to 4:00 PM on weekdays, and anything handed in after 3:20 PM waits until the next business day. That cutoff is earlier than the Recorder's 3:30 PM desk closing, so plan the Auditor stop first.

sections.h2: What does the Hamilton County Recorder charge?
sections.html:
The Recorder lists a flat $34.00 for the first two pages of a deed, mortgage, lease or power of attorney, and $8.00 for each page after that (8 1/2 by 14 inches or a fraction of a page). The office notes that all fees are set by the Ohio General Assembly.

ServiceAmount printed on the Recorder's page
Recording, first two pages$34.00 (minimum fee $34.00)
Recording, each added page$8.00
Certified copy$2.00 per page, plus $1.00 for the seal
Copy made by the public$0.10 per page, self-served
Copy made by staff$2.00 per page
Marginal notation on a release or assignment$4.00, since April 29, 2022
Release of federal tax lien$3.00

Source: Hamilton County Recorder fee schedule and FAQ pages. A document that arrives short on fees is sent back unrecorded. A document that arrives over is recorded and the extra is refunded. Cards are accepted with a convenience charge: $2.00 on a debit card, and on a credit card the greater of $2.00 or 2.39%.

sections.h2: What does the Hamilton County Auditor charge to transfer a deed?
sections.html:
The Auditor's page prints three charges for a taxable transfer in Hamilton County: a state conveyance fee of 1.00 per thousand of the sale price, a county permissive tax of 2.00 per thousand, and a state transfer fee of .50 per parcel. Ask the Transfer Desk to confirm the total for your sale price before you leave the house for the courthouse.

Some transfers owe none of the sale-based fees. The DTE Form 100 EX lists exemptions such as a gift between spouses or between a parent and child, a transfer to an heir or devisee, a deed that only confirms or corrects an earlier recorded deed, and a transfer where no money or other valuable consideration changes hands. The Auditor says an affidavit of facts always goes with two of those exemptions: one that provides or releases security for a debt, and one for a transfer with no consideration that is not a gift.

Two more forms can ride along. DTE Form 101 applies if the seller had the homestead reduction in the preceding or current tax year, and DTE Form 102 applies if the land had a current agricultural use valuation.

sections.h2: Does Hamilton County still have registered (Torrens) land?
sections.html:
Registered land is no longer a separate track in Hamilton County. The Board of Commissioners passed Resolution 25 on August 6, 2014 to abolish it, and since November 10, 2015 any registered land document is recorded in the traditional system at the standard $34.00 and $8.00 rates.

No new certificate of title is issued under that change. A preparer should cite the existing certificate of title as the prior instrument until the parcel has changed hands. The county notes it held more registered land than any other Ohio county, and it has put millions of registered land images online.

If your parcel was ever registered, tell your title company early. Adverse possession cannot run against registered land, which makes the history of such a parcel worth a careful look.

sections.h2: What format must a Hamilton County deed follow before the Recorder accepts it?
sections.html:
Ohio Revised Code 317.114 sets the page standard for every county, and the Recorder's FAQ points to it through its document standardization guidelines. A deed that misses the standard is still recorded, but the statute adds a $10 base fee and a $10 housing trust fund fee.

  • Print no smaller than font size ten, in black or blue ink, with no highlighting.
  • Paper between 8 1/2 by 11 and 8 1/2 by 14 inches.
  • One-inch margins on the sides and across the bottom of each page.
  • A three-inch blank margin across the top of the first page, with the right half reserved for the Recorder's endorsement, and a one and one-half inch blank margin at the top of later pages.

Releases and assignments must carry a full legal description under ORC 5301.46, and a Hamilton County deed that describes the land differently from the last recorded deed may need a boundary survey approved by the County Engineer before the Auditor will transfer it.

sections.h2: Can I protect myself from deed fraud in Hamilton County?
sections.html:
Yes. The Recorder runs a Real Estate Fraud Alert recording notification service at no charge. When a document is recorded under a name or identity you are monitoring, an email goes out to you.

The office's online search, called Acclaim, lets anyone browse the index and document images without paying. For owners who live out of town or hold inherited property, signing up costs nothing and gives early warning of an unexpected filing against the parcel.

faqs.q: Does the Hamilton County Recorder prepare deeds?
faqs.a: No. The Recorder's FAQ says the office does not sell blank forms, and the website says staff cannot run searches or title work for customers. Use an attorney or title company to draft the deed.

faqs.q: Can I mail a deed to the Hamilton County Recorder?
faqs.a: Yes, but only after the Engineer's and Auditor's stamps are on it. Include a self-addressed, stamped envelope so the recorded deed can come back to you.

faqs.q: What time does the Hamilton County recording desk close?
faqs.a: The recording desk closes at 3:30 PM, though the office itself stays open until 4:00 PM. The Auditor's Transfer Desk will not process anything handed in after 3:20 PM until the next business day.

faqs.q: Do I pay the Recorder and the Auditor at the same window?
faqs.a: No. They are separate offices in the same building. The Auditor collects the conveyance and transfer fees, and the Recorder collects the recording fee.

faqs.q: Is recording a deed required after a sale in Hamilton County?
faqs.a: Yes in practice. Under ORC 5301.25 a deed that has not been recorded is treated as fraudulent against a later buyer in good faith who had no knowledge of it, so the new owner's title stays exposed until the Recorder indexes the deed.
